lead.headline: For Soldiers’ Families, Abu Dhabi Brings Hope of a Homecoming
lead.deck: Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large prisoner exchange, though the war goes on.
body: When soldiers are captured in a war, their families can wait a long time for news. On Wednesday there was hopeful news. After two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, which means each side sends captured soldiers home.

The number is not final yet. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said between 1,000 and 1,200 prisoners may be exchanged. Jared Kushner, an American who helped lead the talks, said the numbers would be set on Thursday.

The harder questions were left open. The sides did not agree to a ceasefire, a stop to the fighting, and they still disagree about land. Kushner said, “we are pushing a boulder uphill.” He and Steve Witkoff now go to Moscow to meet Russia’s president, then to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy.

world.headline: At the Climate Summit, a Push to Plug More of Life Into Electricity
world.deck: About 40 leaders spoke in Antalya; many big countries’ leaders stayed away.
body: Think of the things at home that burn fuel: a petrol car, a gas heater, a gas stove. Each could run on electricity instead. At COP31, the United Nations climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, the host country is asking the world to make that switch faster.

Turkey’s idea is a promise called “35 by 35”. Today electricity supplies 23% of the energy the world uses. The promise is to reach 35% by 2035. Thirteen countries, including Australia, Germany and Pakistan, have backed it so far. Joining is a choice.

Not everyone is satisfied. The promise does not say how the electricity should be made, and the Marshall Islands, a Pacific island country, said it is not enough unless the power is clean. About 40 leaders spoke on Wednesday. The United Nations chief, António Guterres, said that fossil fuels “must go the way of the dinosaurs”.

us.headline: American Prices Rose More Than Expected in October
us.deck: Food, electricity and housing all cost more than in September.
body: Every month the US government measures how much prices have changed for things families buy. Tuesday’s report said prices rose 0.4% in October. Experts had expected 0.3%. Food rose 0.5%, and groceries and electricity were among the costs that went up.
Rising prices are called inflation. A bank called the Federal Reserve, or the Fed, tries to slow inflation by raising interest rates. Interest is the extra money people pay when they borrow.
After the report, traders saw an 84% chance that the Fed will raise rates in December. That would make loans for homes cost more.
us.why: Small monthly rises add up in a family’s shopping. A question for the table: what has become dearer at our shops lately?

india.headline: India Will Spend Much More to Keep Fertiliser Affordable for Farmers
india.deck: The winter season’s subsidy rises 64%, to Rs 62,370 crore.
body: Wheat, mustard and pulses are planted in India’s winter season, called Rabi. To grow well, these crops need fertiliser, which feeds plants with nutrients such as phosphate and potash. India buys much of this fertiliser, and the materials to make it, from other countries.

That is a problem when world prices rise, as they have lately. So on Wednesday the Cabinet, the group of senior ministers led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved a subsidy for the season. A subsidy is money the government pays so that something costs less.

The amount is about Rs 62,370 crore, around 64% more than last winter’s. The money goes to fertiliser companies so they can sell to farmers at lower prices. Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said farmers will not face any additional burden. It was one of five plans approved on Wednesday. Another will make the Noida Metro’s Aqua Line 8.45 km longer, with five new stations.
india.why: What farmers pay for fertiliser affects what it costs to grow food, and so what families pay for it.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to The Breakfast Table for Thursday, November 12. Today: soldiers who may be going home, a plan to plug more of life into electricity, and why prices keep creeping up.
Let’s start with the talks in Abu Dhabi. They are over. What came out of them?
One clear thing. After two days, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war. That means each side sends captured soldiers home.
How many people is that?

The number is not final. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said between 1,000 and 1,200 prisoners may be exchanged. An American who helped lead the talks, Jared Kushner, said the numbers would be set on Thursday.
So has the fighting stopped?

No. The two sides did not agree to a ceasefire, and they still disagree about land. Kushner said, we are pushing a boulder uphill. But for families who have waited a long time for news, an exchange is real hope.
What happens next?
Kushner and Steve Witkoff go to Moscow to meet Russia’s president, and then to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy.
Now to the climate summit in Turkey. What is this promise called 35 by 35?

Think of things that burn fuel, like a petrol car or a gas heater. Each could run on electricity instead. Today electricity supplies 23 percent of the energy the world uses. The promise is to reach 35 percent by 2035.
Who has signed up?
Thirteen countries so far, including Australia, Germany and Pakistan. Joining is a choice, not a rule.
Is everyone happy with it?

Not everyone. The promise does not say how the electricity should be made. The Marshall Islands said it is not enough unless the power is clean. And Australia’s climate minister said an electric car cuts emissions by 60 percent on coal power, and 90 percent on solar.
Last one. Prices in the United States went up again?
Yes. A report on Tuesday said prices rose 0.4 percent in October. Experts had expected 0.3 percent. Food rose 0.5 percent.
That sounds small. Why does it matter?

Rising prices are called inflation, and small monthly rises add up in a family’s shopping. A bank called the Federal Reserve tries to slow inflation by raising interest rates. Interest is the extra money people pay when they borrow.
And will it raise them?
Traders saw an 84 percent chance that it will in December. That would make loans for homes cost more.
